items.title: GDC Tips: Intersection of Two Lines

moments.title: Intersection of two lines
moments.text: Find the common point using a simultaneous-equation solver and then by graphing.

moments.title: Identify the common point
moments.text: The intersection lies on both lines, so its coordinates satisfy both equations.

moments.title: Set up the system solver
moments.text: Choose two equations in the variables $x$ and $y$.

moments.title: Graph the same equations
moments.text: Enter the right-hand sides as two functions and display both lines.

moments.title: Find their intersection on the graph
moments.text: Select the intersection tool, then bracket the crossing with bounds on either side.

moments.title: Compare both methods
moments.text: The graphing method gives the same ordered pair as the system solver.

notes.title: Meaning of the solution
notes.text: At the intersection, the formulas give the same output for the same input. The coordinates satisfy both equations.

notes.title: Calculator model
notes.text: The demonstration uses a TI-Nspire. Equivalent tools may be in different menus on another calculator.
notes.write: Use both coordinates as a check.

items.title: GDC Tips: Plotting Functions & Analysis Tools

moments.title: Plotting and analysing a function
moments.text: The presenter introduces graphing and the calculator’s graph-analysis tools.

moments.title: A cannonball’s height
moments.text: A height–time graph is used to ask about maximum height, landing time, initial height and when the ball reaches a given height.

moments.title: Enter the quadratic model
moments.text: Enter $h(t)=-2t^2+20t+8$, using the calculator’s graph variable in place of $t$.

moments.title: The first window hides the graph’s features
moments.text: The default view is too narrow to show the maximum and landing point; change the viewing window.

moments.title: Zoom and set useful bounds
moments.text: Zoom out and adjust the horizontal and vertical bounds to display the parabola’s important features.

moments.title: Maximum height
moments.text: The maximum is $(5,58)$: after $5$ seconds the height is $58$ metres.

moments.title: Landing time from a zero
moments.text: Find the positive zero, approximately $10.4$ seconds. The negative zero lies outside the real-world time interval.

moments.title: Initial height
moments.text: The vertical intercept is $(0,8)$, so the ball starts $8$ metres above ground.

moments.title: Intersect with a horizontal line
moments.text: Graph $y=40$ and find the first intersection at $(2,40)$. The second intersection is $(8,40)$, on the way down.

moments.title: Review the features
moments.text: The presenter revisits the maximum, zero, vertical intercept and intersection as answers to questions about the model.

notes.title: Window versus domain
notes.text: A window such as $-5\leq t\leq15$ helps display the full curve. It does not mean negative time or time after the ball lands is physically meaningful.
notes.write: For this model the meaningful interval is approximately $0\leq t\leq10.4$.

notes.title: One height can occur twice
notes.text: The height $40$ m occurs at $t=2$ and $t=8$ seconds. Read the question carefully: the first time is $2$ seconds, while both times answer when the height is $40$ m.

ican.text: I can identify intercepts, maxima, minima and intersections from a graph or equation.
I can describe where a function increases or decreases and distinguish local from absolute extrema.
I can interpret coordinates, units and domain restrictions in context.
I can use an intersection to solve an equation and check whether all relevant solutions have been found.

ku.text: Intercepts occur where a graph meets an axis. Solve $f(x)=0$ for $x$-intercepts and calculate $f(0)$ for the $y$-intercept if $0$ belongs to the domain.
A maximum or minimum point is an ordered pair. The maximum or minimum value is its output coordinate; the input coordinate says where it occurs.
A local extremum is highest or lowest compared with nearby domain values. An absolute extremum is highest or lowest over the entire domain. Endpoints can be absolute extrema even without a turn.
A function increases over an interval when larger inputs give larger outputs, and decreases when larger inputs give smaller outputs. Read intervals along the input axis.
An intersection of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ satisfies both equations. Its input solves $f(x)=g(x)$; the point includes the common output.
A graph can have several intersections or none. A calculator window may hide a feature, and numerical coordinates are often approximations.
Domain restrictions can remove roots, intersections or turning points from a model. Interpret remaining points using the quantities and units in the question.

misc.better: The maximum value is $9$, attained at input $2$.
It solves $f(x)=g(x)$. It is a root of either function only if the shared output is zero.

misc.weak: A turning point must be the absolute maximum or minimum.
misc.better: Compare its output with all other relevant values, including endpoints and other turning points.

misc.weak: The graph shows only one intersection in the current window.
misc.better: Examine the relevant domain and use algebra or a solver to check for others.

terms.text: An output at least as large as outputs at nearby inputs in the domain.
The smallest output attained across the entire domain under consideration.
An input where the function equals zero. Its associated graph point is an $x$-intercept.
A common point of two graphs. Its coordinates satisfy both equations.

worked.prompt: Consider $f(x)=-(x-2)^2+9$ on the restricted domain $0\leq x\leq5$, and the line $g(x)=x+3$.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the maximum point, maximum value and intervals of increase and decrease.
parts.a: The vertex form gives the maximum point $(2,9)$ and maximum value $9$. The function increases on $[0,2]$ and decreases on $[2,5]$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the intercepts of the restricted graph of $f$.
parts.a: $f(0)=5$, giving $(0,5)$. For roots, $(x-2)^2=9$, so $x=-1$ or $x=5$. Only $x=5$ is in the stated domain, giving $(5,0)$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find the intersections of the two graphs within the domain.
parts.a: Set $-(x-2)^2+9=x+3$, giving $x^2-3x-2=0$. Thus $x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}2$. Only $\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}2\approx3.56$ lies in $[0,5]$. The intersection is approximately $(3.56,6.56)$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: State the absolute minimum of $f$ on the given domain and explain why it is not a turning point.
parts.a: The minimum value is $0$ at $x=5$. This is the right endpoint of the restricted domain; the curve does not turn there.

kq.q: What is the difference between an extremum point and an extremum value?
kq.model: The point includes the input and output, for example $(2,9)$. The maximum value is $9$ and it occurs at input $2$.

kq.q: How does a restricted domain change graph features?
kq.model: Keep only points with permitted inputs. An algebraic root or intersection can disappear, and an endpoint can become an absolute maximum or minimum.

kq.q: Why is an intersection an equation solution?
kq.model: At a shared point the outputs are equal at the same input, so its input satisfies $f(x)=g(x)$.
